objectives: Trace the origins of accounting from Mesopotamian tokens to Pacioli's codification of double-entry bookkeeping.
Apply the accounting equation Assets = Liabilities + Equity to any transaction.
Record a basic transaction using T-accounts with correct debit and credit rules.

slides.title: The ancient roots of accounting — from clay tokens to Roman ledgers
slides.body:
Accounting is as old as civilisation itself. The earliest evidence of systematic record-keeping comes from **Mesopotamia**, where clay tokens were used as early as **8000 BCE** to track commodities such as grain, livestock, and oil. By **3000 BCE**, Sumerian scribes at sites like **Uruk** were impressing cuneiform symbols onto clay tablets to document temple inventories — the ancient equivalent of a warehouse management system. These tablets, many excavated by archaeologists such as **Denise Schmandt-Besserat**, show that before writing was used for literature or law, it was used for accounts.

In **Egypt**, the **New Kingdom** (c. 1550–1070 BCE) saw detailed grain-ledger papyri maintained by royal scribes. The great pharaonic building projects required careful tracking of labour, rations, and materials — a logistics problem that demanded primitive but functional accounting.

The **Romans** formalised matters further. Roman citizens of the equestrian and senatorial class were legally required to maintain two sets of books: the *codex accepti et expensi* (a cash-receipts-and-payments journal) and the *codex rationum domesticorum* (a household account book). Roman bankers — the *argentarii* — kept customer accounts and cleared transactions across the Empire's financial network. The Roman treasury, the **Aerarium Saturni**, employed professional scribes whose record-keeping practices would be broadly recognisable to a modern bookkeeper.

The medieval **Italian city-states** — Venice, Genoa, Florence, and Pisa — drove the next leap. Long-distance sea trade required merchants to track complex webs of credit, agency relationships, and multi-currency transactions. The **Medici family**, whose banking empire under **Cosimo de' Medici** (1389–1464) stretched from Florence to London, Bruges, and Rome, operated with branch-level ledgers that showed assets, liabilities, and profits at each location. The Medici bank's account books, studied by historian **Raymond de Roover**, demonstrate double-entry bookkeeping fully formed by the early fifteenth century — at least fifty years before Pacioli wrote it down.

This long arc — from Sumerian clay tokens through Roman *argentarii* to Florentine bankers — set the stage for the single most important event in the history of accounting: the publication, in 1494, of a book that would teach double-entry bookkeeping to the world.

slides.title: Luca Pacioli, the accounting equation, and how double-entry works
slides.body:
**Luca Pacioli** (c. 1447–1517) was a Franciscan friar, mathematician, and close friend of **Leonardo da Vinci** — who illustrated Pacioli's later book *De Divina Proportione* (1509). In **1494**, Pacioli published *Summa de arithmetica, geometria, proportioni et proportionalità* in Venice. Within that encyclopaedic work was a 27-chapter section, *Particularis de computis et scripturis* ("Details of Accounts and Writings"), which codified the Venetian double-entry method in print for the first time. Pacioli did not invent double-entry bookkeeping — he acknowledged the Venetian merchants who had used it for generations — but he described it so clearly and accessibly that it spread across Europe within decades. For this reason he is universally called the **"Father of Accounting."**

Pacioli's method rests on one foundational insight that has never changed in over five centuries:

**The Accounting Equation:**
$$\text{Assets} = \text{Liabilities} + \text{Equity}$$

Every resource a business owns (**Assets** — cash, inventory, equipment, receivables) was financed by someone. Either a creditor provided it (**Liabilities** — loans, accounts payable, bonds) or the owners provided it (**Equity** — owner's capital, retained earnings). The equation must always balance; it is an identity, not a hypothesis.

**Double-entry** means that every transaction affects at least two accounts, in equal and opposite amounts — so the equation stays in balance after every single entry. The two sides of every entry are called a **debit** and a **credit**:

- **Debit (Dr)**: an entry on the **left** side of a T-account. Debits **increase** Asset and Expense accounts; they **decrease** Liability, Equity, and Revenue accounts.
- **Credit (Cr)**: an entry on the **right** side of a T-account. Credits **increase** Liability, Equity, and Revenue accounts; they **decrease** Asset and Expense accounts.

A handy mnemonic: **DEAD CLIC** — **D**ebits increase **E**xpenses, **A**ssets, and **D**raws; **C**redits increase **L**iabilities, **I**ncome, and **C**apital.

The **T-account** is the visual tool: the account name sits at the top of a "T"; debits are listed on the left branch, credits on the right. The **balance** of the account is the net of the two sides. The viz panel on this slide shows a live ledger: try entering a transaction and watch both sides of the equation move.

Pacioli also insisted on three books: the **memorandum** (rough notes), the **journal** (formal chronological entry of each transaction), and the **ledger** (individual account pages). The journal-to-ledger workflow he described is still used today, five centuries later, in every accounting software system from **QuickBooks** to **SAP S/4HANA**.

slides.title: The accountant's role — from merchant clerks to the modern profession
slides.body:
For most of history, accounting was an occupational skill of clerks, scribes, and merchants — not a recognised profession. That changed during the Industrial Revolution, when the scale and complexity of enterprises — railways, coal mines, textile mills — created a demand for reliable, independent financial reporting.

The modern accounting profession was born in **Scotland**. The **Institute of Accountants in Glasgow** (founded **1853**) and the **Institute of Accountants in Edinburgh** (founded **1854**) were the world's first professional accounting bodies. Their members were the first to use the designation **CA** (Chartered Accountant). In **1880**, the **Institute of Chartered Accountants in England and Wales (ICAEW)** was established by Royal Charter. In the **United States**, the **American Institute of Certified Public Accountants (AICPA)** traces its lineage to the American Association of Public Accountants, formed in **1887**.

The rise of the **joint-stock corporation** — and especially the catastrophic railway share frauds of the 1840s and the subsequent **Companies Act 1862** in the UK — created a legal requirement for audited accounts. The idea: an independent accountant should examine a company's books and certify them as true and fair. This **audit function** became the cornerstone of the profession.

The twentieth century brought further institutionalisation. The **Generally Accepted Accounting Principles (GAAP)** in the United States were gradually formalised, with the **Financial Accounting Standards Board (FASB)** established in **1973** as the independent standard-setter. Internationally, the **International Accounting Standards Committee (IASC)**, founded in **1973**, evolved into the **International Accounting Standards Board (IASB)** in **2001**, which issues **International Financial Reporting Standards (IFRS)** — now adopted by over 140 countries.

The profession's biggest modern scandals — **Enron (2001)**, audited by **Arthur Andersen**, and **WorldCom (2002)** — led directly to the **Sarbanes-Oxley Act (SOX) of 2002**, which created the **Public Company Accounting Oversight Board (PCAOB)** and imposed personal criminal liability on executives who certify false financial statements.

Today, the "Big Four" accounting firms — **Deloitte**, **PricewaterhouseCoopers (PwC)**, **Ernst & Young (EY)**, and **KPMG** — each employ hundreds of thousands of professionals globally and audit the vast majority of large public companies. The accountant's role has expanded far beyond bookkeeping to encompass **financial reporting**, **tax advisory**, **forensic accounting**, **management consulting**, and **ESG assurance** — but the foundation remains the same T-account system that Luca Pacioli described in Venice in 1494.

question.question: Who is called the "Father of Accounting" and why?
options: Cosimo de' Medici (1389–1464), because the Medici bank was the first institution to use double-entry bookkeeping systematically across multiple branches.

Luca Pacioli (c. 1447–1517), because his 1494 work *Summa de arithmetica* contained *Particularis de computis et scripturis*, the first printed, systematic description of double-entry bookkeeping — spreading the Venetian method across Europe and making it the universal foundation of accounting. Pacioli was a Franciscan friar and mathematician, a friend of Leonardo da Vinci, working in Venice. He explicitly credited the Venetian merchants who had developed the method before him.
Raymond de Roover (1904–1972), because his historical research first uncovered the Medici bank's use of double-entry.
The Emperor Augustus, because Roman law required citizens to keep two sets of account books.
question.explanation: Pacioli did not invent double-entry — Venetian and Florentine merchants had practiced it for at least 50 years before he wrote. But his 1494 *Summa* was the first printed, detailed, systematic account of the method. It spread rapidly via the new printing press and became the template for all subsequent bookkeeping instruction. The Medici and the Romans kept records, but neither codified the method for transmission. Raymond de Roover was a twentieth-century historian, not a practitioner.

hints: Think about who put the method into print, not who invented it.
slides.workedSolution: Luca Pacioli (c. 1447–1517) published *Summa de arithmetica, geometria, proportioni et proportionalità* in Venice in 1494. Embedded within it was *Particularis de computis et scripturis*, a 27-chapter description of the Venetian double-entry method. It was the first time the method appeared in print. The book spread via the printing press to German, Dutch, English, and French merchants and became the universal foundation of accounting instruction. Pacioli is therefore called the 'Father of Accounting' — not because he invented the practice, but because he codified and transmitted it.

question.question: A new business has the following at the end of its first week: Cash $12,000; Equipment $8,000; Accounts Payable $5,000; Owner's Capital $15,000. Using the accounting equation $A = L + E$, what is the value of total Assets?
question.hint: Add all assets (Cash + Equipment). Then verify: $A = L + E$ means $A = 5{,}000 + 15{,}000 = 20{,}000$. Both sides must balance.

question.question: Record a transaction using double-entry T-accounts
question.goal: A business buys office supplies for $400 cash. Record this transaction by identifying which accounts are affected, which side (debit or credit) each moves, and confirm the accounting equation still balances.

steps.prompt: Which two accounts are affected by buying supplies for cash?
steps.motivation: Every double-entry transaction touches at least two accounts.
hints: One account represents what you received; the other represents what you gave up.
steps.reveal: The two accounts are **Supplies** (an asset you received) and **Cash** (an asset you gave up). Both are asset accounts — this is an asset-for-asset swap, which is perfectly common.

steps.prompt: Which account is debited and which is credited? By how much?
steps.motivation: Applying debit/credit rules: debits increase assets, credits decrease assets.
hints: DEAD CLIC: Debits increase Assets. Supplies is going up — it gets debited. Cash is going down — it gets credited.
steps.reveal: **Debit Supplies $400** (asset increases — left side of T-account). **Credit Cash $400** (asset decreases — right side of T-account). Total debits = $400 = Total credits = $400. The entry balances.

steps.prompt: After this entry, does the accounting equation A = L + E still hold? (Assume Assets were $20,000, Liabilities $5,000, Equity $15,000 before the transaction.)
steps.motivation: Double-entry guarantees the equation always balances.
hints: One asset went up $400, another went down $400 — net change to total assets is zero.
steps.reveal: Yes. Supplies +$400 and Cash −$400 cancel out exactly. Total assets remain $20,000. Liabilities and Equity are untouched. $20,000 = $5,000 + $15,000. The equation holds. This is the guarantee that double-entry provides: every correctly recorded transaction leaves the equation in balance.

question.prompt: In ≤150 words, explain double-entry bookkeeping to someone who has never studied accounting. Use the accounting equation, give one concrete example of a transaction, and say why the system was revolutionary when Pacioli described it in 1494.
question.rubric: Should clearly state the accounting equation Assets = Liabilities + Equity. Should explain that every transaction produces at least two entries — a debit and a credit — that keep the equation balanced. Should give a concrete transaction example (e.g., borrowing cash creates an asset on one side and a liability on the other). Should mention Luca Pacioli and 1494. Should convey why this was revolutionary: systematic self-checking (the trial balance catches errors), portability via the printing press, enabling complex multi-branch enterprises like the Medici bank, and the separation of ownership from day-to-day record-keeping. Bonus: mention that it enabled arm's-length investment and joint-stock companies.
